content.text: This guide is for engineers managing feature flags in the Orbit platform.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide § text#0

content.text: It details the process of rolling out a feature flag from off to fully on, outlining prerequisites for each step.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide § text#5

content.text: The guide explicitly excludes the process for experiments, indicating a separate, undefined process.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide § text#6

content.text: Each section of the guide will detail specific conditions that must be met before advancing the feature flag to the next stage of rollout.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide § text#8

content.text: The flag is active only for staff accounts, allowing internal identification of problems before customer exposure. This stage typically lasts one working day, with no minimum duration specified.

content.text: A small percentage (5%) of real traffic is exposed to the change, chosen randomly per request. This stage must last at least 30 minutes to cover a full traffic cycle of the slowest endpoint. Manual percentage changes during this period restart the measurement window. Short canaries are a common cause of problematic flags reaching general availability.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#1

content.text: The flag advances from canary only if an automated metrics check passes. This check compares the error rate and p95 latency of flagged requests against the previous 7 days. If it fails, the flag remains in canary for investigation. The rollout tool automatically runs this check at the end of the canary window.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#2

content.text: The flag is progressively turned on for everyone in steps of 25%, 50%, and 100%. During this ramp-up, the owner monitors the error dashboard and pages the on-call engineer if errors increase. The dashboard displays flagged and unflagged requests side-by-side to distinguish flag-related issues from platform issues. Monitoring continues until the flag has been at 100% for one hour.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#3

content.text: Each stage of the rollout is recorded in the rollout tool, which maintains a history of who moved the flag and when.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#4

content.text: The rollout process is a sequential flow designed to minimize customer impact from new features. It progresses through internal testing, a controlled canary release, and finally a phased general availability. A critical automated check acts as a gatekeeper between canary and general availability, preventing problematic flags from reaching a wider audience. The process emphasizes monitoring at each stage, with specific conditions for advancement and failure.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#5

content.text: The most common reason for a bad flag reaching general availability is a short canary stage, which can lead to insufficient metric collection and analysis.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#6

content.text: The rollout process ensures that new features are gradually exposed to users, with safeguards and monitoring in place to detect and mitigate issues before they affect a large user base.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Rollout stages ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Advancing from canary ⨁ Feature flag rollout guide › Monitoring during general availability § text#7

content.text: Every feature flag must include a kill switch capable of deactivating the flag within 1 minute.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#0

content.text: The kill switch must be tested in the staging environment before the flag proceeds to canary. This test must be documented in the rollout tool.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#1

content.text: A feature flag cannot be deployed to the canary environment if its kill switch has not been tested.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#2

content.text: Any member of the owning team is authorized to activate the kill switch without requiring prior approval.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#3

content.text: Deactivating a feature flag via its kill switch is always a safe operation. Re-enabling a flag will restart its rollout process from the internal stage.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#4

content.text: The kill switch ensures rapid deactivation of feature flags, providing a safety mechanism. This is critical for mitigating risks associated with new features.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#5

snapshot.content: Analysis · Impact of Untested Kill Switch

content.text: The requirement for testing the kill switch in staging and recording it in the rollout tool prevents flags with unverified safety mechanisms from reaching production environments.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Kill switch § text#6

content.text: A flag is removed from the code after being fully on for 30 days.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Flag cleanup § text#0

content.text: The flag owner creates a cleanup ticket when the flag reaches 100% rollout. This ticket must link to the rollout record.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Flag cleanup § text#1

content.text: Flags that are not removed by their deadline are included in the weekly stale-flag report.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Flag cleanup § text#2

content.text: Keeping old flags in the codebase negatively impacts code readability and slows down future rollouts.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Flag cleanup § text#3

content.text: This flow outlines the process for removing feature flags from the codebase once they are no longer needed. The goal is to maintain code hygiene and efficiency.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Flag cleanup § text#4

content.text: If a flag is not removed within the specified timeframe (30 days after being fully on), it will be flagged in a weekly report, indicating a deviation from the cleanup process.

ai.stableNodeKey: Feature flag rollout guide › Flag cleanup § text#5
